title: What Does World Modeling Actually Improve in Robot Action Learning?

paper.title: What Does World Modeling Actually Improve in Robot Action Learning?
paper.abstract:
Abstract World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts.
We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family.
Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively.
Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns.
However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision.
We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%.
These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine vision-language pretraining with robot data to learn policies that generate actions from visual observations and language instructions [ 17 , 10 , 8 , 4 ] . Building on this foundation, World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate future visual prediction into action learning, training models to predict environmental changes alongside robot actions. Methods such as GR-1, GR-2, PAD, and InternW0 integrate these objectives through different architectures, demonstrating the potential of future prediction to support robot action learning [ 13 , 6 , 9 , 5 ] . However, improvements in task success alone do not reveal which aspects of policy execution benefit from predictive supervision, nor do they establish that the model has acquired transferable understanding of its environment. Prior work provides an important starting point for understanding these effects. Fast-WAM separately examines video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger drop in action performance [ 14 ] . This finding supports the value of predictive supervision during training, but final success rates do not reveal how the gains manifest in execution behavior or to what extent they persist across models, tasks, and environments. Rather than simply revisiting whether video prediction improves task success, we investigate where the benefits of predictive supervision appear and under which conditions they persist. This distinction matters for assessing the practical value of future prediction and determining how such supervision should be used in subsequent model designs. To investigate these questions, we conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM. Within each family, we keep the architecture, initialization, robot training data, and number of training steps fixed, varying only whether the future-video prediction loss is included. We first evaluate execution success on seen tasks under clean conditions. We then use trajectory clustering to examine changes in the frequencies of coarse trajectory patterns and their within-cluster success rates, providing behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success. We further vary task identity and environment configuration separately to assess whether the gains persist on unseen tasks and under environmental randomization. Together, these comparisons distinguish improvements in familiar-task execution, observable changes in behavior, and the conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial. These analyses also raise a practical design question: if future-video prediction provides useful training supervision, does obtaining its benefits necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation model? To examine this, we introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for the existing VLA model π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] . We compare the original policy with variants equipped with either a lightweight Transformer predictor or a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch. Both auxiliary prediction branches are used only during training and removed at inference. This comparison tests whether a lightweight predictor can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT branch. Figure 1 summarizes our research questions, experimental design, and main findings. Figure 1 : Overview and main findings. (a) Controlled comparison with and without future-video prediction loss, using identical architectures within each WAM family. (b) Representative behavior-mode analysis on FastWAM’s stack_blocks_two task: the dominant mode M0 retains a similar frequency, while its within-mode success rate increases from 50.2% to 89.5%. Scatter layouts and point colors are schematic; numerical annotations report measured statistics. (c) Success-rate differences between λ video = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1 and λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 for FastWAM and OpenWAM under Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized conditions (Experiment 3). The Seen task set differs from Experiment 1. (d) Adding a training-only lightweight video predictor improves π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} success rate from 82.94% to 89.19%, compared with 86.97% using a pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B branch. Our experiments reveal a clear distinction between the benefits of predictive supervision and the conditions under which they persist. Across ten seen tasks under clean conditions, adding the future-video prediction loss increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, demonstrating substantial execution gains in both WAM families. Trajectory analysis further shows that within-cluster success rates increase for several coarse trajectory clusters even when their frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in shifts in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks depend on the model and task, while both WAMs exhibit low absolute success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, with no consistent advantage from predictive supervision. For π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the training-only lightweight predictor increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that auxiliary prediction can provide positive gains in this setting without a large pretrained video DiT branch. These findings indicate that future-video prediction can provide effective supervision for action learning, but its benefits on familiar tasks, their manifestations in execution behavior, and their persistence under distribution shifts must be evaluated separately rather than inferred from aggregate success alone. The lightweight auxiliary predictor further shows that obtaining benefits from future prediction does not necessarily require a large video-generation backbone. Our results therefore provide empirical guidance for selecting training objectives in future WAMs and VLAs: predictive supervision should be evaluated in terms of its observed execution gains and the conditions under which they hold, rather than assuming that predictive capability, transfer performance, and prediction-model scale are necessarily linked.

sections.heading: Future Prediction in Robot Action Learning.
sections.text: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future visual prediction with action generation, enabling robot policies to model future environmental changes alongside control actions. GR-1 and GR-2 integrate video pretraining with joint prediction of future visual observations and robot actions [ 13 , 6 ] , while PAD jointly models future images and actions through a denoising process [ 9 ] . InternW0 adopts an asymmetric architecture, using a high-capacity video expert to model visual dynamics and a lighter action expert for control [ 5 ] . These approaches illustrate different ways of combining future prediction with action learning, but the role of predictive information differs across systems. An important distinction is whether future prediction serves as auxiliary supervision during training or explicitly informs action generation at inference time. The former influences learning through an additional prediction objective, whereas the latter uses predicted future observations or intermediate goals to guide subsequent actions. For example, CoT-VLA generates visual subgoals at inference time and uses them as intermediate conditions for action prediction [ 16 ] . These two approaches can coexist within a single system, but their contributions to action performance should be distinguished. Our study focuses on the benefits of adding a future-video prediction loss during training, rather than planning with explicitly predicted future states at inference.

sections.heading: Understanding the Role of Predictive Supervision.
sections.text: Beyond developing joint visual prediction and action generation models, recent studies have examined the specific contributions of future prediction within WAMs. Fast-WAM separately investigates video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger decline in action performance [ 14 ] . This provides direct evidence for the value of predictive supervision during training. OpenWAM systematically studies design choices involving generative backbones, visual representations, world-action interactions, and training strategies, examining how different configurations affect world-action learning [ 12 ] . Together, these studies highlight that WAM performance depends not only on future prediction but also on architectural choices, information exchange, and training configurations. It is therefore important to distinguish performance differences between complete systems from the contribution of a specific predictive training objective. Although Fast-WAM demonstrates that video co-training improves action performance in its system, aggregate success rates alone do not reveal how these gains manifest in execution behavior. Higher success may accompany changes in the frequencies of different trajectory patterns or arise within similar trajectory patterns. Likewise, improvements on familiar tasks do not establish whether the benefits persist under task or environmental changes. We extend this line of investigation through controlled future-video prediction loss comparisons within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM, complemented by coarse-grained trajectory analysis and evaluations under distribution shifts. Our study characterizes the execution gains, observable behavioral differences, and conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial, without attributing these observations to a specific internal control mechanism.

sections.heading: Auxiliary Prediction and Model Design.
sections.text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models improve robot policies through vision-language pretraining, robot data, and action generation objectives. RT-2 explores transferring vision-language knowledge to robotic control [ 17 ] , while OpenVLA, Open X-Embodiment, and Octo advance generalist policy learning from heterogeneous robot datasets [ 10 , 11 , 8 ] . For action generation, π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow matching to model continuous actions, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further combines heterogeneous co-training with high-level semantic prediction to improve performance in open-world settings [ 4 , 3 ] . The high-level semantic prediction in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} differs in its supervision target from the future-video prediction studied here. We investigate whether adding future visual prediction to an existing VLA training setup can provide useful auxiliary supervision for action learning. Future prediction need not involve direct RGB video generation. In visual representation learning, V-JEPA learns representations by predicting masked video features rather than reconstructing pixels [ 2 ] . V-JEPA 2 further scales video representation learning and develops an action-conditioned latent world model for robotic planning [ 1 ] . Within world-action modeling, ImageWAM explores image-editing priors as an alternative to dense video generation [ 15 ] . These studies illustrate different choices of prediction targets and model architectures, although they do not directly establish which predictive design is most beneficial for action learning. Motivated by these alternatives, we further examine future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for an existing VLA. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we compare a lightweight Transformer predictor with a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch, focusing on whether auxiliary prediction can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT. Because the two branches differ in architecture and training configuration, this comparison evaluates the feasibility of lightweight auxiliary prediction rather than isolating model scale as the cause of performance differences.

sections.heading: 3 Study Design
sections.text: This section describes how we isolate the contribution of future-video prediction supervision to action learning. We first define the controlled variable and comparison logic, then specify task and environment conditions, and finally describe the three types of evidence used throughout the study. Figure 2 illustrates the two auxiliary video-prediction configurations for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Figure 2 : Training configurations for auxiliary video prediction in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . (a) A randomly initialized six-layer Transformer predicts future-video latent flow conditioned on projected shared VLM representations, with targets encoded by a frozen Wan2.2 VAE. (b) A pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT predicts future-video latent flow conditioned on adapted VLM representations and frozen T5 text features; the DiT is trainable, while the VAE and T5 encoder are frozen. Both variants retain the original action pathway and use the video branch only during training, removing it at inference. The video objective updates the shared vision-language pathway and the corresponding prediction branch, but does not directly update the action expert, which is trained by the action objective.

sections.heading: 3.1 Controlled Variable: The Video Prediction Loss
sections.text: We compare two training-objective configurations separately within FastWAM and OpenWAM. Both configurations use the same visual observations, language instructions, and action supervision; only the weight of the future-video prediction loss differs: ℒ = ℒ action + λ video ​ ℒ video . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{video}}. (1) When λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 , training uses only the action loss; when λ video = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1 , it uses both losses. This ablation does not change the model architecture or parameter count: within each family, the two settings share the same initialization, module-freezing configuration, and training steps. Two clarifications are important. First, setting λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 disables the explicit future-video prediction loss; it does not remove the world-model architecture or its visual representations. Second, we repeat the same comparison across two model families to test whether the observed benefit is confined to a single implementation. Absolute performance differences between FastWAM and OpenWAM should not be treated as a controlled architecture comparison, because the two families differ in pretraining, model size, and training pipeline. Beyond the WAM experiments, we extend auxiliary video prediction to the VLA policy π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , comparing the original policy with two training-time auxiliary predictors. The design and results for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} are presented separately in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Tasks, Environments, and Evaluation Conditions
sections.text: All experiments use bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0 [ 7 ] for training. The training set contains 40 tasks, with 45 demonstrations per task used for training and five reserved for validation. Tasks designated for Unseen evaluation are excluded from training. Evaluation involves four condition dimensions. Seen tasks have their task identity present in the training data; evaluation uses held-out initial states distinct from training, so it tests execution from new starting configurations rather than replaying training episodes. Unseen tasks have their task identity entirely excluded from training, testing cross-task transfer. Clean environments match the standard scene configuration used during training. Randomized environments alter visual and scene configurations at test time, probing robustness to environmental perturbation. The three WAM experiments use different task sets—an important prerequisite for interpreting the results. Experiment 1 evaluates seen-task gains on ten Seen tasks. Experiment 2 analyzes trajectory behavior on a separate set of five tasks (only open_laptop overlaps with Experiment 1). Experiment 3 uses a distinct set of five Seen tasks and ten Unseen tasks to evaluate performance under distribution shift. Absolute success rates should not be compared across experiments.

sections.heading: 3.3 Evidence Types and Analysis Protocols
sections.text: We employ three types of evidence, each addressing a different aspect of predictive supervision.

sections.heading: Within-family success-rate comparison.
sections.text: We report the success-rate difference Δ ​ SR = SR ⁡ ( λ video = 1 ) − SR ⁡ ( λ video = 0 ) \Delta\mathrm{SR}=\mathrm{SR}(\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1)-\mathrm{SR}(\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0) within each model family. Experiment 1 evaluates ten Seen tasks in Clean environments with 3,200 rollouts per setting. Experiment 3 extends the evaluation to the four Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized conditions, yielding 19,200 rollouts per family.

sections.heading: Trajectory-level behavior decomposition.
sections.text: Changes in aggregate success can arise from entering different coarse trajectory modes or from higher success within similar modes. To distinguish the two, Experiment 2 pools trajectories from both loss settings within each task and clusters them using numerical trajectory features; model identity, scene identity, and success labels are excluded from clustering. We then compare mode frequencies and within-mode success rates. Each model family contributes 12,800 trajectories across five tasks. The resulting clusters are coarse trajectory patterns, not semantically verified strategies.

sections.heading: Benefit persistence under distribution shift.
sections.text: The Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized grid in Experiment 3 tests whether the gains observed on familiar tasks extend to unseen tasks and altered environments. For the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} experiments, three variants are each evaluated with 3,200 rollouts sharing matched initial observations and action noise. We report success-rate changes relative to the original policy with paired scene-level bootstrap confidence intervals. The detailed protocol is described alongside the architecture in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: 4 What Does Predictive Supervision Change?
sections.text: This section presents the three WAM experiments, organized around three progressive questions: how large is the benefit of predictive supervision on familiar tasks, how does it manifest in execution behavior, and whether it persists under distribution shift.

This provides behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success rates: the benefit is not limited to changing which trajectory modes are selected; it also appears as higher success within similar execution patterns. These modes are clusters of numerical trajectory features, and some may partly reflect scene geometry. We therefore interpret them as descriptive behavioral statistics, not as evidence of a specific causal mechanism. Both experiments so far evaluate familiar conditions within the training distribution. A key follow-up question is whether these gains persist when tasks or environments change.

sections.heading: Cross-task benefits are model- and task-dependent.
sections.text: Under Unseen+Clean, FastWAM gains only 0.28 points, whereas OpenWAM still gains 23.38 points. The OpenWAM gain, however, is concentrated in a subset of tasks: place_container_plate , open_microwave , and press_stapler improve by 52.50, 71.88, and 73.44 points, respectively, while other unseen tasks improve little or decline slightly. Predictive supervision thus has some cross-task transfer value, but the effect is strongly task- and model-dependent.

sections.heading: No stable benefit under environment randomization.
sections.text: Under Randomized conditions, absolute success rates are low for both families (at most 3.22%), and the changes from adding the prediction loss are small and negative (FastWAM: − 0.13 -0.13 / − 1.62 -1.62 pp; OpenWAM: − 0.25 -0.25 / − 2.75 -2.75 pp). Because of the severe floor effect, these negative differences do not establish that the λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}{=}0 setting is more robust. Equally, no positive advantage from predictive supervision is observed under these conditions. These results reveal a noteworthy contrast: a training objective that produces substantial gains on familiar tasks does not automatically confer reliable transfer under the evaluated environmental shifts. Predictive supervision can improve action learning near the training distribution, but seen-task execution gains and robust transfer are distinct targets that should not substitute for each other in evaluation. The three experiments establish an empirical picture of predictive supervision: it is a valuable training signal whose benefits have clear boundaries. This motivates a design-level question: must one incorporate a large pretrained video-generation branch to obtain such training benefits in an existing VLA policy? We address this question in the next section through auxiliary-prediction experiments on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .

sections.heading: 5 From Understanding to Design: Auxiliary Prediction for VLA
sections.text: The preceding experiments show that future-video prediction supervision provides a valuable training signal for action learning, though its benefits concentrate near the training distribution and vary across tasks and models. These findings raise a design-level question: can a VLA policy that was not built as a world–action model also benefit from a training-time auxiliary prediction branch, and must that branch be a large pretrained video-generation model? We address this question through three π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} configurations.

sections.heading: 5.1 Design Question and Auxiliary Prediction Variants
sections.text: We compare three configurations: the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , a variant augmented with a lightweight Transformer video predictor, and a variant using pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B as the auxiliary video-prediction branch. All three retain the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action pathway unchanged. In the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , a trainable SigLIP encoder processes the current three-view RGB observations and combines them with language instructions and robot state to form shared vision-language prefix representations. The action expert then predicts continuous actions through flow matching. In both augmented variants, the video-prediction branch reads context from the shared prefix. Gradients from the video objective propagate through each branch into the shared vision-language prefix and visual pathway, but do not directly update the private action expert. Both video branches are used only during training and are removed at inference, so action generation does not require explicit future-video prediction.

sections.heading: Lightweight Transformer branch.
sections.text: The 2,048-dimensional shared-prefix hidden states are projected to 512 dimensions through a trainable context projection and normalization layer, then fed into a randomly initialized six-layer Transformer with eight attention heads. Supervision is constructed in the latent space of a frozen Wan2.2 VAE: the explicit inputs to the video head are noisy future latents together with the corresponding video timestep, while current-observation information is supplied through the shared prefix. Training uses a flow-matching loss; the video-loss coefficient increases linearly from 0 to 0.1 over the first 1,000 optimizer steps and remains at 0.1 thereafter.

sections.heading: Wan2.2-TI2V-5B branch.
sections.text: The shared prefix is mapped into the Wan conditioning space through a trainable 2,048-to-4,096 prefix adapter. The same language instruction is additionally encoded and cached offline by a frozen T5 encoder and concatenated with the adapted prefix along the token dimension to condition the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT. The Wan DiT remains trainable during this experiment; the VAE and T5 encoder are frozen. The branch receives clean current latents and noisy future latents, computing the video loss only on the future latents. Its external video-loss coefficient is one throughout training, with loss weighting prescribed by the Wan scheduler.

sections.heading: Training-condition matching.
sections.text: The original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and the lightweight variant share the same initialization, robot training split, seed (42), action optimizer, effective batch size (32), and 50,000-step training budget; the lightweight branch is the only additional component. The Wan-based variant is also evaluated from its 50,000-step checkpoint with seed 42, but differs in auxiliary architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, scheduler, and loss weighting. The lightweight-versus-original comparison is therefore a relatively controlled paired experiment, while comparisons involving the Wan branch are complementary rather than a strict ablation of video-model size or pretraining.

sections.heading: 5.3 Results and Design Implications
sections.text: All three variants are evaluated on the same ten Seen tasks with 100 fixed scenes, 32 rollouts per scene per variant (3,200 rollouts each), sharing initial observations and matched action noise indexed by rollout and action chunk. Using paired scene-level bootstrap within tasks, the 95% confidence interval for the lightweight-minus-original difference is [ 2.31 , 10.31 ] [2.31,10.31] percentage points, and the interval for Wan-minus-original is [ 0.16 , 8.22 ] [0.16,8.22] points. Both intervals lie above zero, supporting positive aggregate gains for both auxiliary-prediction variants on the evaluated task set. The lightweight predictor achieves a 2.22-point higher aggregate success rate than the Wan variant, but the 95% confidence interval for the Wan-minus-lightweight difference is [ − 5.63 , 1.25 ] [-5.63,1.25] and includes zero. The lightweight variant therefore has the highest point estimate, yet the current evaluation does not establish a statistically reliable advantage over the Wan variant. Per-task results further show that the relative performance of the two approaches is strongly task-dependent: Wan attains the highest point estimate on tasks such as place_a2b_right and place_dual_shoes , while the lightweight predictor performs better on open_laptop and pick_diverse_bottles . These results support two conditional design implications. First, the benefit of auxiliary video prediction is not confined to dedicated WAM architectures; it extends to a conventional VLA policy. Both auxiliary variants improve π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on the evaluated tasks, indicating practical value of training-time predictive supervision as a general auxiliary objective. Second, in the current setting, obtaining the training benefit of auxiliary prediction does not require a large pretrained video DiT. The lightweight Transformer does not load a pretrained Wan DiT yet improves substantially over the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . However, the lightweight variant still uses video latents from a frozen Wan2.2 VAE as prediction targets; the result therefore does not show that pretrained video representations are unnecessary altogether. Moreover, the lightweight and Wan branches differ simultaneously in architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, and loss weighting, so the current comparison cannot attribute performance differences to model size alone.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: The preceding experiments establish a set of empirical facts about future-video prediction supervision: it substantially improves action learning on familiar tasks, its benefits manifest in execution behavior beyond aggregate success rates, it does not reliably persist under distribution shift, and obtaining such training benefits does not necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation branch. We distill these facts into three interrelated design insights and then discuss the limitations of the current evidence.

sections.heading: Training-objective gains and transferability should be evaluated separately.
sections.text: This is the central observation of the paper. Under Seen+Clean conditions, predictive supervision yields gains of +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, with both families showing consistent positive effects. However, when evaluation extends to unseen tasks and randomized environments, the picture changes markedly: FastWAM gains almost nothing under Unseen+Clean, OpenWAM’s cross-task gains concentrate in a subset of tasks, and both models exhibit near-zero absolute success rates under environmental randomization. This contrast indicates that a training objective capable of substantially improving in-distribution performance cannot automatically serve as a proxy for generalization. For model evaluation, researchers reporting the effects of predictive supervision—or any training objective—should present results near the training distribution and under explicit shift conditions separately, rather than inferring the latter from the former. For model design, improving in-distribution execution and achieving out-of-distribution transfer may require different technical mechanisms; a single predictive training objective should not be expected to address both.

sections.heading: Aggregate success rates do not capture the full behavioral impact.
sections.text: Trajectory clustering reveals that, on several tasks, coarse trajectory-mode frequencies remain nearly unchanged while within-mode success rates increase substantially. This provides a meaningful clue beyond aggregate metrics: the benefit of predictive supervision is not limited to changing which trajectory modes the policy selects; it also appears as higher success within similar execution patterns. The interpretive boundary of this evidence must also be acknowledged. The clusters are based on numerical trajectory features, and some may partly reflect scene geometry rather than distinct control strategies. We have not measured action precision, force control, or specific kinematic indicators, so we cannot determine what changes occur in the model’s internal action representations or fine-grained control capabilities. For future work, WAM and VLA evaluation should not be limited to final success rates. Trajectory- and behavior-level analyses can reveal benefit patterns that aggregate metrics miss, but establishing stronger causal explanations will require finer-grained behavioral characterization tools and targeted interventional experiments.

sections.heading: The value of a predictive training objective should not be conflated with the necessity of a large generator.
sections.text: The π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} experiments show that a randomly initialized six-layer lightweight Transformer predictor, without loading a pretrained Wan DiT, increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. This offers a meaningful reference for engineering decisions: when future prediction primarily serves as training-time auxiliary supervision, the benefit does not necessarily require an expensive large-scale video-generation backbone. Two important qualifications apply. First, the lightweight variant still uses latents from a frozen Wan2.2 VAE as prediction targets, so it has not entirely dispensed with pretrained video representations; whether a specific target representation space is needed, and how its quality affects the benefit, requires further independent study. Second, the lightweight and Wan branches differ simultaneously in architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, and loss weighting, so the current comparison cannot attribute performance differences to model size alone. The 2.22-point success-rate gap between the two, with a 95% confidence interval that includes zero, does not support a statistically reliable advantage for either variant. The current conclusion is therefore that a large pretrained video DiT is not a necessary prerequisite for obtaining auxiliary-prediction training benefits in the evaluated π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} setting. Whether specific tasks, data scales, or pretraining conditions make a large video model necessary remains an open question.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The following limitations affect the interpretive scope of our findings. The WAM controlled experiments are based on a single training run per configuration. Although each configuration is evaluated with thousands of rollouts, rollout-level variation does not equal training-seed-level stability. The results support incremental trends within the tested configurations but do not confirm their reproducibility across multiple independent training seeds. Under environment randomization, both models achieve low absolute success rates across all conditions. This floor effect limits our ability to distinguish between “predictive supervision does not help robustness” and “the current models lack the overall capability for these conditions.” The trajectory clustering analysis uses coarse numerical features and may incorporate scene-geometry differences into mode assignments. The results reflect statistical changes in trajectory behavior and should not be treated as causal identification of internal control mechanisms. We have not reported systematic comparisons of end-to-end training cost, GPU memory usage, or inference latency among the three π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} configurations. Differences in parameter count do not directly translate to differences in training efficiency or deployment feasibility. Finally, all experiments are conducted on bimanual manipulation tasks in the RoboTwin 2.0 simulation platform. Whether the findings generalize to different robot embodiments, real-world environments, or larger-scale training data remains to be examined in future work.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Through controlled experiments, we investigate the practical role of future-video prediction supervision in robot action learning. Within the FastWAM and OpenWAM families, predictive supervision produces substantial execution gains on familiar tasks, and trajectory-level analysis provides behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success rates. However, these gains do not reliably persist on unseen tasks or under environmental randomization, indicating that improvements on familiar tasks and robust transfer are distinct targets that must be evaluated separately. For π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , a training-only lightweight predictor achieves positive gains, showing that effective auxiliary predictive supervision does not necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation branch in the evaluated setting. These results provide empirical guidance for training-objective selection in WAMs and VLAs: future-video prediction is a valuable form of training supervision, but its execution benefits, behavioral manifestations, and transfer capabilities should be examined as separate dimensions. Translating these benefits into reliable out-of-distribution generalization remains an open research challenge.

sections.heading: 8 Detailed Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: This section provides additional details of the evaluation protocols used in the main paper. Experiments 1–3 compare controlled No-WM and WM variants within FastWAM and OpenWAM in order to isolate the effect of future-video prediction supervision as much as possible. Experiment 4 serves as a complementary extension on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and compares different future-video prediction designs rather than a strictly architecture-matched No-WM/WM pair.

sections.heading: 8.1 Experiment 1: Seen+Clean Evaluation
sections.text: Experiment 1 evaluates whether future-video prediction supervision improves action success under Seen+Clean conditions. OpenWAM is evaluated on ten Seen+Clean tasks with ten fixed initial states per task and 32 rollouts per state for each model variant, resulting in 3,200 rollouts per method. FastWAM is likewise evaluated on ten Seen+Clean tasks with 3,200 valid rollouts per method.

sections.heading: 8.2 Experiment 2: Behavior-Mode Analysis
sections.text: Experiment 2 analyzes how the performance differences observed in Experiment 1 are reflected in trajectory-level behavior. For both FastWAM and OpenWAM, we evaluate five tasks with ten fixed scenes per task and collect 128 complete trajectories per scene from each of No-WM and WM. This results in 1,280 trajectories per task and method, and 12,800 trajectories in total for each model family. For each task, trajectories from all ten scenes and both model variants are pooled to construct a shared set of candidate behavior modes from numerical trajectory features. Model identity, success labels, and scene identity are excluded from clustering and mode construction. After clustering, we measure the frequency of each mode and the success rate conditioned on that mode for each model variant. These modes are candidate clusters derived from numerical trajectory features rather than semantically validated action strategies. We therefore use Experiment 2 as a descriptive behavioral analysis and do not interpret the resulting clusters as definitive semantic strategy classes. For the four rigid-object tasks, trajectories are expressed in an object-centric frame: positions are translated by the manipulated-object center and horizontally aligned using the direction from the object’s initial position to its target. Features include gripper–object contact location and object identity, end-effector orientation, the final 15 cm of the pre-contact path, up to 48 steps or 10 cm of the post-contact path, relative gripper-closing time, and the delay between the first contacts of the two arms. Path features are resampled by arc length. Only contacts between the manipulated object and fl/fr_link7 or link8 are retained; table, base, and robot self-contacts are excluded. For open_laptop , the articulated-object base pose was unavailable, so trajectories are translated using the initial object–table contact centroid but are not rotation-aligned. An arm with no valid object contact retains a binary no-contact indicator, while its position, orientation, path, and relative contact-time features are set to zero so that the static geometry of an inactive arm does not dominate clustering. Each feature dimension is centered by its task-level median, scaled by its standard deviation with a floor of 0.05, and clipped to [ − 6 , 6 ] [-6,6] . Feature groups are additionally weighted by the inverse square root of their dimensionality. We do not normalize each scene independently. We apply K-means separately to each task after pooling both model variants and all ten scenes. Candidate values K = 2 , … , 8 K=2,\ldots,8 are ranked by silhouette score, subject to a minimum cluster size of 32 trajectories. If the best silhouette score is below 0.15, a single cluster is retained. Neither model identity, scene identity, nor success labels enter the features or the selection criterion. Stability is diagnosed using adjusted Rand index over three additional clustering seeds and leave-one-scene-out refits. These choices define an exploratory candidate-mode analysis rather than a statistical test for a natural number of semantic strategies.

sections.heading: 8.3 Experiment 3: Distribution Shift
sections.text: Experiment 3 examines whether the gains from future-video prediction supervision persist under task-level and environment-level distribution shifts. We evaluate five Seen tasks and ten Unseen tasks that are completely held out from training, with ten fixed initial states per task. The evaluation varies along two independent dimensions: whether the task is represented in the robot training data and whether the environment is randomized. Their Cartesian product defines four evaluation conditions: Seen+Clean, Seen+Randomized, Unseen+Clean, and Unseen+Randomized. Both FastWAM and OpenWAM sample 32 rollouts per state for each model variant. This results in 1,600 rollouts per method for each Seen condition and 3,200 rollouts per method for each Unseen condition. Across both model variants and all four conditions, the complete evaluation contains 19,200 rollouts for each model family.

sections.heading: 8.4 Experiment 4: Extension to pi0.5
sections.text: Experiment 4 examines whether the benefit of future-video prediction supervision extends to a conventional VLA policy that is not explicitly designed as a WAM. We compare three variants based on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} : the original policy, a variant augmented with a lightweight future-video predictor, and a variant using pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B as the video-prediction module. All three models are evaluated on the same ten Seen tasks, with ten fixed scenes per task and 32 stochastic policy repetitions per scene. This results in 320 rollouts per task and model, and 3,200 rollouts in total for each model. The three models use the same fixed scenes and initial observations together with matched action noise derived from rollout and action-chunk identity, yielding a paired evaluation protocol. Action inference uses an action horizon of 32, 24 replanning steps, and ten action-sampling steps. Because all tasks contain the same number of scenes and rollouts, the macro-average success rate across the ten tasks is identical to the aggregate success rate over all 3,200 rollouts. The original and lightweight-video variants use the same pi05_base initialization, robot training split, seed 42, and 50,000 optimizer updates. Both use four GPUs, four samples per GPU, and two-step gradient accumulation, giving an effective batch size of 32. Optimization uses AdamW with cosine learning-rate decay from 2.5 × 10 − 5 2.5\times 10^{-5} to 2.5 × 10 − 6 2.5\times 10^{-6} , 1,000 warmup steps, weight decay 0.01, global-norm clipping at 1.0, and EMA decay 0.999. The lightweight branch is the only additional component in that paired training run. The Wan-based policy is evaluated from its 50,000-step EMA checkpoint trained with seed 42. Its auxiliary branch differs in architecture, initialization, conditioning, scheduler weighting, and video-loss coefficient, so comparisons involving Wan are treated as extension results rather than a strictly matched causal ablation.

sections.text: This section reports complete per-task results for Experiment 3 in Sec. 4.3 . Results are reported under the four combinations of Seen/Unseen tasks and Clean/Randomized environments. The task-level results reveal substantial model- and task-dependent variation in how the gains from future-video prediction supervision transfer across distributions.

sections.heading: 11.1 FastWAM

sections.heading: 12 Extension to pi0.5
sections.text: This section provides additional details on the training setup, implementation, and results of the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} extension in Experiment 4. The overall structures of the two future-video prediction variants are illustrated in the main-paper architecture figure, while this section records the module, gradient, and loss details needed for reproducibility.

sections.heading: 12.1 Architecture and Training Details
sections.text: All three variants retain the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action pathway, where the current three-view RGB observations are encoded by a trainable SigLIP image encoder and combined with instruction and robot-state information to form shared vision-language prefix representations before continuous actions are generated by the action expert through flow matching. Both auxiliary video branches read context from the shared prefix, allowing gradients from the video objective to update the shared vision-language representation without directly updating the private action expert. In the lightweight video-auxiliary variant, the 2048-dimensional prefix hidden states are first mapped to 512 dimensions through a trainable context projection and normalization layer. A randomly initialized six-layer Transformer with a hidden dimension of 512 and eight attention heads then serves as the video-prediction network and contains both self-attention and cross-attention. The video supervision is constructed in the latent space of the frozen Wan2.2 VAE. The frozen VAE is used offline to encode a nine-frame video window containing the current and future three-view observations, from which the two future latent temporal blocks are used as prediction targets. The explicit latent input to the video head consists of noisy future latents together with the corresponding video timestep, while information about the current observation is supplied through the shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} prefix. The total objective of the lightweight variant combines the action loss with a weighted video loss, where the video-loss coefficient is linearly increased from 0 to 0.1 over the first 1,000 optimizer steps and remains fixed at 0.1 thereafter. In the Wan-based variant, the shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} prefix is first mapped into the Wan conditioning space through a trainable 2048-to-4096 prefix adapter. The same language instruction is additionally encoded and cached offline by a frozen T5 encoder and is concatenated with the adapted prefix along the token dimension to condition the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT. All parameters of the Wan DiT remain trainable during this experiment, while the Wan2.2 VAE and T5 encoder are frozen. The video input is formed by concatenating a clean current latent and noisy future latents along the video-time dimension, with the current latent assigned timestep zero, while the video loss is computed only over the future latent targets. The Wan-based variant uses an external video-loss coefficient of one from the first training step together with the scheduler-dependent training weight defined by the Wan video objective and does not use a step-based warmup. In both variants, gradients from the video objective propagate through the corresponding video branch into the shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} prefix and visual pathway. The SigLIP encoder and shared vision-language backbone receive gradients from both the action and video objectives, the private action expert and action output head are updated only by the action objective, and the video head, Wan DiT, and their corresponding projection layers are updated only by the video objective. Table 13 : Gradient and inference roles of the main components in the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} video-auxiliary variants. Component Action Loss Video Loss Used at Inference SigLIP + shared VLM backbone Yes Yes Yes Action expert + action head Yes No Yes Video head / Wan DiT + adapters No Yes No Frozen VAE / frozen T5 No No No Both video-auxiliary branches are used only during training and are removed during action inference. At test time, only the trained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} image encoder, shared vision-language backbone, action expert, and action output head are retained, so action generation does not require explicit future-video prediction. Importantly, the lightweight and Wan-based variants differ simultaneously in video-prediction architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, scheduler, and loss weighting. We therefore do not interpret their performance difference as a strict causal ablation of model size or pretrained prior.

sections.text: All three π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} configurations are evaluated on the same ten Seen tasks and 100 fixed scenes, with 32 rollouts per scene and model. The original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} achieves a success rate of 82.94%, the lightweight future-video predictor increases the success rate to 89.19%, and the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B variant reaches 86.97%. Jie Cao Affiliation: MAIS & NLPR, Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences * Equal contribution Project lead Corresponding author Abstract World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting. 1 Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine vision-language pretraining with robot data to learn policies that generate actions from visual observations and language instructions [ 17 , 10 , 8 , 4 ] . Building on this foundation, World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate future visual prediction into action learning, training models to predict environmental changes alongside robot actions. Methods such as GR-1, GR-2, PAD, and InternW0 integrate these objectives through different architectures, demonstrating the potential of future prediction to support robot action learning [ 13 , 6 , 9 , 5 ] . However, improvements in task success alone do not reveal which aspects of policy execution benefit from predictive supervision, nor do they establish that the model has acquired transferable understanding of its environment. Prior work provides an important starting point for understanding these effects. Fast-WAM separately examines video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger drop in action performance [ 14 ] . This finding supports the value of predictive supervision during training, but final success rates do not reveal how the gains manifest in execution behavior or to what extent they persist across models, tasks, and environments. Rather than simply revisiting whether video prediction improves task success, we investigate where the benefits of predictive supervision appear and under which conditions they persist. This distinction matters for assessing the practical value of future prediction and determining how such supervision should be used in subsequent model designs. To investigate these questions, we conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM. Within each family, we keep the architecture, initialization, robot training data, and number of training steps fixed, varying only whether the future-video prediction loss is included. We first evaluate execution success on seen tasks under clean conditions. We then use trajectory clustering to examine changes in the frequencies of coarse trajectory patterns and their within-cluster success rates, providing behavioral evidence beyond aggregate success. We further vary task identity and environment configuration separately to assess whether the gains persist on unseen tasks and under environmental randomization. Together, these comparisons distinguish improvements in familiar-task execution, observable changes in behavior, and the conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial. These analyses also raise a practical design question: if future-video prediction provides useful training supervision, does obtaining its benefits necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation model? To examine this, we introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for the existing VLA model π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] . We compare the original policy with variants equipped with either a lightweight Transformer predictor or a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch. Both auxiliary prediction branches are used only during training and removed at inference. This comparison tests whether a lightweight predictor can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT branch. Figure 1 summarizes our research questions, experimental design, and main findings. Figure 1 : Overview and main findings. (a) Controlled comparison with and without future-video prediction loss, using identical architectures within each WAM family. (b) Representative behavior-mode analysis on FastWAM’s stack_blocks_two task: the dominant mode M0 retains a similar frequency, while its within-mode success rate increases from 50.2% to 89.5%. Scatter layouts and point colors are schematic; numerical annotations report measured statistics. (c) Success-rate differences between λ video = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1 and λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 for FastWAM and OpenWAM under Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized conditions (Experiment 3). The Seen task set differs from Experiment 1. (d) Adding a training-only lightweight video predictor improves π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} success rate from 82.94% to 89.19%, compared with 86.97% using a pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B branch. Our experiments reveal a clear distinction between the benefits of predictive supervision and the conditions under which they persist. Across ten seen tasks under clean conditions, adding the future-video prediction loss increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, demonstrating substantial execution gains in both WAM families. Trajectory analysis further shows that within-cluster success rates increase for several coarse trajectory clusters even when their frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in shifts in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks depend on the model and task, while both WAMs exhibit low absolute success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, with no consistent advantage from predictive supervision. For π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the training-only lightweight predictor increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that auxiliary prediction can provide positive gains in this setting without a large pretrained video DiT branch. These findings indicate that future-video prediction can provide effective supervision for action learning, but its benefits on familiar tasks, their manifestations in execution behavior, and their persistence under distribution shifts must be evaluated separately rather than inferred from aggregate success alone. The lightweight auxiliary predictor further shows that obtaining benefits from future prediction does not necessarily require a large video-generation backbone. Our results therefore provide empirical guidance for selecting training objectives in future WAMs and VLAs: predictive supervision should be evaluated in terms of its observed execution gains and the conditions under which they hold, rather than assuming that predictive capability, transfer performance, and prediction-model scale are necessarily linked. 2 Related Work Future Prediction in Robot Action Learning. World Action Models (WAMs) combine future visual prediction with action generation, enabling robot policies to model future environmental changes alongside control actions. GR-1 and GR-2 integrate video pretraining with joint prediction of future visual observations and robot actions [ 13 , 6 ] , while PAD jointly models future images and actions through a denoising process [ 9 ] . InternW0 adopts an asymmetric architecture, using a high-capacity video expert to model visual dynamics and a lighter action expert for control [ 5 ] . These approaches illustrate different ways of combining future prediction with action learning, but the role of predictive information differs across systems. An important distinction is whether future prediction serves as auxiliary supervision during training or explicitly informs action generation at inference time. The former influences learning through an additional prediction objective, whereas the latter uses predicted future observations or intermediate goals to guide subsequent actions. For example, CoT-VLA generates visual subgoals at inference time and uses them as intermediate conditions for action prediction [ 16 ] . These two approaches can coexist within a single system, but their contributions to action performance should be distinguished. Our study focuses on the benefits of adding a future-video prediction loss during training, rather than planning with explicitly predicted future states at inference. Understanding the Role of Predictive Supervision. Beyond developing joint visual prediction and action generation models, recent studies have examined the specific contributions of future prediction within WAMs. Fast-WAM separately investigates video co-training during training and future generation at inference, finding that removing the former leads to a larger decline in action performance [ 14 ] . This provides direct evidence for the value of predictive supervision during training. OpenWAM systematically studies design choices involving generative backbones, visual representations, world-action interactions, and training strategies, examining how different configurations affect world-action learning [ 12 ] . Together, these studies highlight that WAM performance depends not only on future prediction but also on architectural choices, information exchange, and training configurations. It is therefore important to distinguish performance differences between complete systems from the contribution of a specific predictive training objective. Although Fast-WAM demonstrates that video co-training improves action performance in its system, aggregate success rates alone do not reveal how these gains manifest in execution behavior. Higher success may accompany changes in the frequencies of different trajectory patterns or arise within similar trajectory patterns. Likewise, improvements on familiar tasks do not establish whether the benefits persist under task or environmental changes. We extend this line of investigation through controlled future-video prediction loss comparisons within two WAM families, FastWAM and OpenWAM, complemented by coarse-grained trajectory analysis and evaluations under distribution shifts. Our study characterizes the execution gains, observable behavioral differences, and conditions under which predictive supervision remains beneficial, without attributing these observations to a specific internal control mechanism. Auxiliary Prediction and Model Design. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models improve robot policies through vision-language pretraining, robot data, and action generation objectives. RT-2 explores transferring vision-language knowledge to robotic control [ 17 ] , while OpenVLA, Open X-Embodiment, and Octo advance generalist policy learning from heterogeneous robot datasets [ 10 , 11 , 8 ] . For action generation, π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow matching to model continuous actions, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further combines heterogeneous co-training with high-level semantic prediction to improve performance in open-world settings [ 4 , 3 ] . The high-level semantic prediction in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} differs in its supervision target from the future-video prediction studied here. We investigate whether adding future visual prediction to an existing VLA training setup can provide useful auxiliary supervision for action learning. Future prediction need not involve direct RGB video generation. In visual representation learning, V-JEPA learns representations by predicting masked video features rather than reconstructing pixels [ 2 ] . V-JEPA 2 further scales video representation learning and develops an action-conditioned latent world model for robotic planning [ 1 ] . Within world-action modeling, ImageWAM explores image-editing priors as an alternative to dense video generation [ 15 ] . These studies illustrate different choices of prediction targets and model architectures, although they do not directly establish which predictive design is most beneficial for action learning. Motivated by these alternatives, we further examine future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for an existing VLA. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we compare a lightweight Transformer predictor with a pretrained Wan DiT video-generation branch, focusing on whether auxiliary prediction can improve action performance without introducing a large pretrained video DiT. Because the two branches differ in architecture and training configuration, this comparison evaluates the feasibility of lightweight auxiliary prediction rather than isolating model scale as the cause of performance differences. 3 Study Design This section describes how we isolate the contribution of future-video prediction supervision to action learning. We first define the controlled variable and comparison logic, then specify task and environment conditions, and finally describe the three types of evidence used throughout the study. Figure 2 illustrates the two auxiliary video-prediction configurations for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Figure 2 : Training configurations for auxiliary video prediction in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . (a) A randomly initialized six-layer Transformer predicts future-video latent flow conditioned on projected shared VLM representations, with targets encoded by a frozen Wan2.2 VAE. (b) A pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT predicts future-video latent flow conditioned on adapted VLM representations and frozen T5 text features; the DiT is trainable, while the VAE and T5 encoder are frozen. Both variants retain the original action pathway and use the video branch only during training, removing it at inference. The video objective updates the shared vision-language pathway and the corresponding prediction branch, but does not directly update the action expert, which is trained by the action objective. 3.1 Controlled Variable: The Video Prediction Loss We compare two training-objective configurations separately within FastWAM and OpenWAM. Both configurations use the same visual observations, language instructions, and action supervision; only the weight of the future-video prediction loss differs: ℒ = ℒ action + λ video ​ ℒ video . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{video}}. (1) When λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 , training uses only the action loss; when λ video = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1 , it uses both losses. This ablation does not change the model architecture or parameter count: within each family, the two settings share the same initialization, module-freezing configuration, and training steps. Two clarifications are important. First, setting λ video = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0 disables the explicit future-video prediction loss; it does not remove the world-model architecture or its visual representations. Second, we repeat the same comparison across two model families to test whether the observed benefit is confined to a single implementation. Absolute performance differences between FastWAM and OpenWAM should not be treated as a controlled architecture comparison, because the two families differ in pretraining, model size, and training pipeline. Beyond the WAM experiments, we extend auxiliary video prediction to the VLA policy π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , comparing the original policy with two training-time auxiliary predictors. The design and results for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} are presented separately in Sec. 5 . 3.2 Tasks, Environments, and Evaluation Conditions All experiments use bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0 [ 7 ] for training. The training set contains 40 tasks, with 45 demonstrations per task used for training and five reserved for validation. Tasks designated for Unseen evaluation are excluded from training. Evaluation involves four condition dimensions. Seen tasks have their task identity present in the training data; evaluation uses held-out initial states distinct from training, so it tests execution from new starting configurations rather than replaying training episodes. Unseen tasks have their task identity entirely excluded from training, testing cross-task transfer. Clean environments match the standard scene configuration used during training. Randomized environments alter visual and scene configurations at test time, probing robustness to environmental perturbation. The three WAM experiments use different task sets—an important prerequisite for interpreting the results. Experiment 1 evaluates seen-task gains on ten Seen tasks. Experiment 2 analyzes trajectory behavior on a separate set of five tasks (only open_laptop overlaps with Experiment 1). Experiment 3 uses a distinct set of five Seen tasks and ten Unseen tasks to evaluate performance under distribution shift. Absolute success rates should not be compared across experiments. 3.3 Evidence Types and Analysis Protocols We employ three types of evidence, each addressing a different aspect of predictive supervision. Within-family success-rate comparison. We report the success-rate difference Δ ​ SR = SR ⁡ ( λ video = 1 ) − SR ⁡ ( λ video = 0 ) \Delta\mathrm{SR}=\mathrm{SR}(\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=1)-\mathrm{SR}(\lambda_{\mathrm{video}}=0) within each model family. Experiment 1 evaluates ten Seen tasks in Clean environments with 3,200 rollouts per setting. Experiment 3 extends the evaluation to the four Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized conditions, yielding 19,200 rollouts per family. Trajectory-level behavior decomposition. Changes in aggregate success can arise from entering different coarse trajectory modes or from higher success within similar modes. To distinguish the two, Experiment 2 pools trajectories from both loss settings within each task and clusters them using numerical trajectory features; model identity, scene identity, and success labels are excluded from clustering. We then compare mode frequencies and within-mode success rates. Each model family contributes 12,800 trajectories across five tasks. The resulting clusters are coarse trajectory patterns, not semantically verified strategies. Benefit persistence under distribution shift. The Seen/Unseen × \times Clean/Randomized grid in Experiment 3 tests whether the gains observed on familiar tasks extend to unseen tasks and altered environments. For the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} experiments, three variants are each evaluated with 3,200 rollouts sharing matched initial observations and action noise. We report success-rate changes relative to the original policy with paired scene-level bootstrap confidence intervals. The detailed protocol is described alongside the architecture in Sec. 5 . 4 What Does Predictive Supervision Change? This section presents the three WAM experiments, organized around three progressive questions: how large is the benefit of predictive supervision on familiar tasks, how does it manifest in execution behavior, and whether it persists under distribution shift. 4.1 Strong Gains on Familiar Tasks We begin with the most basic question: does adding the future-video prediction loss improve execution success on tasks seen during training? Table 1 reports the paired comparison on ten Seen+Clean tasks. FastWAM improves from 14.97% to 39.34% (+24.38 percentage points); OpenWAM improves from 7.00% to 79.91% (+72.91 points). We address this question in the next section through auxiliary-prediction experiments on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . 5 From Understanding to Design: Auxiliary Prediction for VLA The preceding experiments show that future-video prediction supervision provides a valuable training signal for action learning, though its benefits concentrate near the training distribution and vary across tasks and models. These findings raise a design-level question: can a VLA policy that was not built as a world–action model also benefit from a training-time auxiliary prediction branch, and must that branch be a large pretrained video-generation model? We address this question through three π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} configurations. 5.1 Design Question and Auxiliary Prediction Variants We compare three configurations: the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , a variant augmented with a lightweight Transformer video predictor, and a variant using pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B as the auxiliary video-prediction branch. All three retain the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action pathway unchanged. In the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , a trainable SigLIP encoder processes the current three-view RGB observations and combines them with language instructions and robot state to form shared vision-language prefix representations. The action expert then predicts continuous actions through flow matching. In both augmented variants, the video-prediction branch reads context from the shared prefix. Gradients from the video objective propagate through each branch into the shared vision-language prefix and visual pathway, but do not directly update the private action expert. Both video branches are used only during training and are removed at inference, so action generation does not require explicit future-video prediction. 5.2 Branch Architectures Lightweight Transformer branch. The 2,048-dimensional shared-prefix hidden states are projected to 512 dimensions through a trainable context projection and normalization layer, then fed into a randomly initialized six-layer Transformer with eight attention heads. Supervision is constructed in the latent space of a frozen Wan2.2 VAE: the explicit inputs to the video head are noisy future latents together with the corresponding video timestep, while current-observation information is supplied through the shared prefix. Training uses a flow-matching loss; the video-loss coefficient increases linearly from 0 to 0.1 over the first 1,000 optimizer steps and remains at 0.1 thereafter. Wan2.2-TI2V-5B branch. The shared prefix is mapped into the Wan conditioning space through a trainable 2,048-to-4,096 prefix adapter. The same language instruction is additionally encoded and cached offline by a frozen T5 encoder and concatenated with the adapted prefix along the token dimension to condition the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B DiT. The Wan DiT remains trainable during this experiment; the VAE and T5 encoder are frozen. The branch receives clean current latents and noisy future latents, computing the video loss only on the future latents. Its external video-loss coefficient is one throughout training, with loss weighting prescribed by the Wan scheduler. Training-condition matching. The original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and the lightweight variant share the same initialization, robot training split, seed (42), action optimizer, effective batch size (32), and 50,000-step training budget; the lightweight branch is the only additional component. The Wan-based variant is also evaluated from its 50,000-step checkpoint with seed 42, but differs in auxiliary architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, scheduler, and loss weighting. The lightweight-versus-original comparison is therefore a relatively controlled paired experiment, while comparisons involving the Wan branch are complementary rather than a strict ablation of video-model size or pretraining. 5.3 Results and Design Implications All three variants are evaluated on the same ten Seen tasks with 100 fixed scenes, 32 rollouts per scene per variant (3,200 rollouts each), sharing initial observations and matched action noise indexed by rollout and action chunk. Both auxiliary variants improve π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on the evaluated tasks, indicating practical value of training-time predictive supervision as a general auxiliary objective. Moreover, the lightweight and Wan branches differ simultaneously in architecture, initialization, conditioning pathway, and loss weighting, so the current comparison cannot attribute performance differences to model size alone. 6 Discussion The preceding experiments establish a set of empirical facts about future-video prediction supervision: it substantially improves action learning on familiar tasks, its benefits manifest in execution behavior beyond aggregate success rates, it does not reliably persist under distribution shift, and obtaining such training benefits does not necessarily require a large pretrained video-generation branch. We distill these facts into three interrelated design insights and then discuss the limitations of the current evidence. Training-objective gains and transferability should be evaluated separately. This is the central observation of the paper. Under Seen+Clean conditions, predictive supervision yields gains of +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points for FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively, with both families showing consistent positive effects. However, when evaluation extends to unseen tasks and randomized environments, the picture changes markedly: FastWAM gains almost nothing under Unseen+Clean, OpenWAM’s cross-task gains concentrate in a subset of tasks, and both models exhibit near-zero absolute success rates under environmental randomization. This contrast indicates that a training objective capable of substantially improving in-distribution performance cannot automatically serve as a proxy for generalization. For model evaluation, researchers reporting the effects of predictive supervision—or any training objective—should present results near the training distribution and under explicit shift conditions separately, rather than inferring the latter from the former. For model design, improving in-distribution execution and achieving out-of-distribution transfer may require different technical mechanisms; a single predictive training objective should not be expected to address both. Aggregate success rates do not capture the full behavioral impact. Trajectory clustering reveals that, on several tasks, coarse trajectory-mode frequencies remain nearly unchanged while within-mode success rates increase substantially. This provides a meaningful clue beyond aggregate metrics: the benefit of predictive supervision is not limited to changing which trajectory modes the policy selects; it also appears as higher success within similar execution patterns. The interpretive boundary of this evidence must also be acknowledged. The clusters are based on numerical trajectory features, and some may partly reflect scene geometry rather than distinct control strategies. We have not measured action precision, force control, or specific kinematic indicators, so we cannot determine what changes occur in the model’s internal action representations or fine-grained control capabilities. For future work, WAM and VLA evaluation should not be limited to final success rates. Trajectory- and behavior-level analyses can reveal benefit patterns that aggregate metrics miss, but establishing stronger causal explanations will require finer-grained behavioral characterization tools and targeted interventional experiments. The value of a predictive training objective should not be conflated with the necessity of a large generator. The π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} experiments show that a randomly initialized six-layer lightweight Transformer predictor, without loading a pretrained Wan DiT, increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%.
